source.title: Transcoders Beat Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability
source.authors: Gonçalo Paulo; Stepan Shabalin; Nora Belrose

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates whether sparse-coder features in language models are interpretable, using automated interpretability scores rather than testing toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reconstruction, sparse-probing, feature-absorption, and feature-density results. These do not directly measure the versions about capacity-driven superposition, canonical SAE units, or feature dimensionality, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a methods comparison between transcoders/skip transcoders and SAEs. SAEs serve as the comparator for the authors' own architecture. The paper reports autointerp scores but includes no neuron baseline and no measure of features spread across neurons. Its results do not bear on whether superposition or sparse recoverable features exist in LLMs; they show only which sparse coder yields more interpretable latents.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Authors find (skip) transcoder latents more interpretable than SAE latents. Skip transcoders Pareto-dominate SAEs on reconstruction (CE loss increase) vs interpretability. They recommend shifting from SAEs on MLP outputs to (skip) transcoders. They report similar, noisy absorption and similar feature density.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK sparse autoencoders and transcoders on LLM activations or MLP input-output behavior; it does not reproduce the toy-network feature-superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Explanation accuracy varies across activation quantiles; SAE scores are lower than transcoder and skip-transcoder scores in the reported comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: On the same models and data, transcoder/skip-transcoder latents score higher on autointerp than SAE latents, e.g. pythia-160m fuzzing 74.6 vs 85.4/86.4. SAE explanation accuracy also drops faster at lower activation quantiles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training objective of a sparse dictionary (reconstruct activations vs reconstruct MLP output) changes how interpretable and monosemantic its latents are.

record.code_released: The paper says training code is available in the sparsify GitHub repo, but gives no URL in the text.
record.problems: The autointerpretability scores rely on Llama 3.1 70b as explainer and scorer and evaluate a limited set of latents (500 for fuzzing and detection; 50 for simulation). The paper describes absorption results as noisy. The reported comparisons do not establish that SAE latents are complete, stable, or canonical units.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A Tables 2-4 report variance explained, ∆ NLL, sparse probing, and absorption. These were not extracted because they do not directly measure the V4 claim about interpretable sparse dictionary features; the paper itself distinguishes sparse probing as information selection and describes absorption results as noisy. Appendix B reports feature-density plots but not a result testing the listed versions.

untested.parts: Toy-model geometry, sparsity-dependent transition; no toy models trained.
Whether LLM features are spread across neurons or recoverable by dictionaries beyond a neuron baseline; the paper only compares sparse-coder architectures.
Completeness, stability, canonicality of SAE features; no seed or size stability analysis.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. SAEs are the comparator for the authors' proposed architecture, and autointerp scores without a neuron baseline don't bear on V4's existence claim. Simulation used only 50 latents; explainer and scorer are both Llama 3.1 70b. Table 1 is flattened, so the column alignment for SST-only models was inferred.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.

The study evaluates sparse-coder feature interpretability in LLMs, but does not test whether features are spread across many neurons or establish that the features it finds are the model's underlying features.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features.
Whether the represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAE latents on the tested Pythia, Llama, and Gemma models
reader_labels.reason: SAE latents receive reported automated interpretability scores across the tested models (r1-r15), providing evidence that sparse dictionary features can be interpreted in LLMs.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: SAE explanation accuracy declines faster across quantiles than transcoder and skip-transcoder explanation accuracy (r16).
